meta.blurb: Leila keeps losing her keys and her words, and she spends all day at a desk. When her nephew Ravi, who studies the brain, comes to stay, he takes her out walking and explains what movement may really do for memory, focus and mood.
meta.bible: Leila: a fifty-five-year-old bookkeeper in a small town, kind and a little worried about her memory. Ravi: her nephew, twenty-six, a neuroscience student who stays with her for a month and explains the brain on daily walks along the Canal path. The town has a Canal, a Market square and a community hall with a dance class. Key terms: Neuron, Synapse, Hippocampus, Aerobic, BDNF, Cortisol, Endorphins, Dementia, Randomised trial, Moderate, Vigorous. The science is real and hedged: much of the work on BDNF and new brain cells comes from animals; studies in people are often small or mixed; exercise helps but is not a cure or a guarantee; no invented numbers or studies. Guideline used: adults are advised to aim for about one hundred and fifty to three hundred minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening on two days (the World Health Organization advice). Voice: friendly, curious, honest about what is not known. Nobody gets personal medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: Leila has lost her keys for the third time this week, and today she forgot a colleague's name. She sits at a desk all day, and she wonders if her memory is getting worse.
Her nephew Ravi arrives for a month, with a rucksack and a head full of science. He studies the brain at university, and he says that moving the body may help the mind.
Ravi says the human brain has about eighty-six billion nerve cells, called neurons. Each one makes thousands of tiny connections with other neurons, which are called synapses.
When you learn something new, some of your connections grow stronger. Scientists call this plasticity, and it means that the brain can keep changing at any age.
The brain is only about two percent of your body weight, but it uses about a fifth of your energy. All of that fuel and oxygen is delivered by the blood.
On their first morning walk beside the canal, Leila's heart begins to beat faster. Ravi says that during exercise more blood flows through the brain, bringing it more oxygen.

Ravi says that aerobic exercise means any steady activity that makes your heart and breathing work harder for a while. Brisk walking, cycling and swimming all count, and you can choose the one you enjoy.
Ravi says that the brain is full of tiny blood vessels, and that they need to stay healthy. What protects the heart in general tends to protect these vessels too.
Ravi tells her about a protein called BDNF, which seems to help nerve cells grow and connect. Exercise raises it in animals and probably in people, but we do not know how much that matters.
Deep in the brain is the hippocampus, which helps you to form new memories. Some studies of older adults have found that regular walking is linked with a slightly larger hippocampus.
In mice that run on wheels, scientists see new brain cells growing in the hippocampus. Whether adult people grow many new cells is still debated, and Ravi is careful to say so.
Ravi explains that people who exercise often have sharper thinking, but that does not prove exercise is the cause. They may also eat well, sleep well and have more money.
When people are chosen by chance to exercise, the results are more modest and more mixed. Many reviews suggest a small benefit for thinking skills in some adults, but not in everyone.
Ravi says that the clearest effects in trials are often on planning, attention and switching between tasks. Scientists call these skills executive function, and they help us to organise a busy day.
After half an hour of brisk walking, Leila feels lighter than she has felt for months. Ravi says that exercise has real effects on mood, and that these are some of the best-supported ones.
Some people feel happy after exercise, and endorphins are often given the credit. Scientists now think that other chemicals in the body may also play a part, and the full story is not clear.
Stress makes the body release a hormone called cortisol. Exercise raises it for a short time, but over weeks it may help the body to cope with stress better.

Ravi says that many studies show exercise can ease symptoms of mild to moderate depression in some people. It is not a replacement for treatment, and anyone with long-lasting low mood should see a doctor.
On Thursday they walk through the park, where the trees make the whole world feel quiet. Some studies suggest that green places calm us more than streets do, although the research is still growing.
Ravi says that a single burst of exercise can briefly improve attention afterwards. In school studies, active breaks have helped children to focus, though the effects are usually small.
Ravi points out that Leila sits for eight hours a day. Long sitting is linked to poorer health, so he suggests that she stand up and move for a few minutes every half hour.
At work the next day, Leila sets a timer on her phone to ring every thirty minutes. Each time it rings, she gets up, fills a glass of water or walks along the corridor.
Leila notices that she falls asleep faster after a day with a long walk. Ravi says that exercise tends to help sleep, and that good sleep helps the brain to store memories.

Ravi shows her the advice of the World Health Organization. Adults are encouraged to do about one hundred and fifty to three hundred minutes of moderate activity every week, plus muscle work on two days.
Ravi explains how to know what moderate exercise feels like. You should be able to talk, but not to sing, while a vigorous effort leaves you able to say only a few words.
Ravi says that muscle exercises are important for more than muscles. Some trials suggest that strength training may improve thinking skills in older adults, though more research is needed.
Leila joins a dance class at the community hall on Tuesday evening. She has to remember steps, listen to the music and watch her partner all at the same time.
Ravi says that learning a new skill makes the brain work in new ways. Steps that feel awkward today become easy after practice, as the connections between your neurons get stronger.
Ravi says that not everyone enjoys vigorous exercise, and that is fine. Gentle activities such as tai chi and yoga may improve balance and mood, according to small studies.
Leila asks her neighbour Mrs Okoro to join their walk, and they chat all the way round the park. Ravi says that good friendships seem to be good for the brain as well.
Leila wants to learn some Italian before a holiday. Ravi says that a few small studies suggest that exercise soon after studying may help memories to last, but more research is needed.
Ravi suggests that Leila writes a short diary each evening about her walks, sleep and mood. He says that a diary is not proof, but it can show patterns that are easy to forget.
Ravi tells Leila that forgetting a name or losing keys is very common at any age. If memory problems become worse, or begin to disturb daily life, she should talk to a doctor.
Large studies link regular physical activity with a lower risk of dementia later in life. This is an association and not a guarantee, because many factors play a part.
Ravi says that exercise is only one of many things that matter. Doctors also mention healthy blood pressure, good hearing, not smoking, learning and having friends.
Ravi says that there is no single brain food that works miracles. A varied diet and enough water are the best advice, because even mild thirst can make it harder to concentrate.
One day it rains hard and the canal path is full of puddles. Leila turns on the radio, dances around the kitchen and climbs the stairs twenty times.
Leila worries that ten minutes is too short to matter. Ravi replies that all movement counts, and that health guidelines say that some activity is better than none.
Ravi says that short, hard bursts of exercise may raise brain chemicals more in some studies. For most people, however, regular moderate exercise is enough, and it is easier to keep up.
Ravi reminds Leila that anyone with a health problem should check with a doctor before starting. Start slowly, and stop and seek help if you feel chest pain, dizziness or severe breathlessness.
Ravi teaches her a balance game: stand on one leg while you brush your teeth. Good balance helps to prevent falls, which become more serious as people grow older.
Ravi says that people keep doing the things that they enjoy. Leila stops forcing herself to do exercises that she hates, and she chooses the ones that make her smile.
Ravi says that habits form best when you link them to something you already do. Leila decides to walk right after her morning coffee, and in one study a new habit took about two months to form.
Leila catches a cold and misses a whole week of walking. Ravi tells her not to feel guilty, and to start again gently when she feels well.
After four weeks, Leila realises that she has not lost her keys for ten days. Ravi is pleased, but he reminds her that sleep, mood and attention could all be part of the reason.
Ravi reminds her that exercise is not a smart pill. Its effects on thinking are modest, and sleep, learning, healthy food and friends all matter just as much.
Ravi says that scientists are not sure that brain-training games help in everyday life. Learning a real new skill, such as a language or an instrument, keeps the mind active and is a lot more fun.
At the end of the month, Ravi catches the train home, and Leila waves from the platform. She promises him that she will keep walking and keep writing in her notebook.
Back at home, Leila makes a plan and sticks it on the fridge. It includes brisk walks, strength exercises twice a week, her dance class, early nights and time with friends.

On Sunday, Ravi calls, and Leila tells him that she has just finished a long walk beside the canal. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor about your own health.
C1C2: Leila stood at her front door and turned out her bag for the third time that week, with a rising sense of embarrassment. That afternoon she had forgotten the name of a colleague she had known for years, and the word had come back only on the bus home. Fifty-five years old and tied to a desk, she began to wonder whether this was what getting older was going to feel like.

The next day her nephew Ravi arrived with a rucksack on his back and a month of holiday ahead of him. He was twenty-six, a student of neuroscience, and he listened to her worries with the calm interest of someone who truly enjoys the subject. Movement may help the brain, he told her, and he promised her that he would explain the evidence honestly, including the parts that nobody has worked out yet.

On their first evening, Ravi drew a sketch on the back of an envelope, explaining that the human brain contains roughly eighty-six billion nerve cells called neurons. Each neuron reaches out to thousands of others through tiny junctions called synapses, so that the whole organ is a web of connections too dense for anyone to picture. Every thought, memory or movement, he said, is a pattern of signals travelling through this web.

Learning, Ravi explained, is not a matter of filing facts away in a cabinet, but of strengthening some connections and letting others fade. Scientists call this quality plasticity, and they now believe that, although it is stronger in youth, the brain keeps changing at every age. Leila found this remarkably comforting, because it meant that her habits might still have something to say about her mind.

Although the brain accounts for only about two percent of body weight, Ravi told her, it burns through roughly a fifth of the energy the body uses at rest. It cannot store much fuel, so it depends on a constant supply of oxygen and sugar delivered by the blood, every second of the day. Anything that helps the circulation, he suggested, might therefore be worth a close look.

They set off along the canal path at a brisk pace, and within ten minutes Leila's heart was thumping and her cheeks were warm. Ravi pointed out that this was exactly the point, because during exercise the heart pumps harder, and measurements show that blood flow to some areas of the brain increases. More blood means more oxygen and fuel, he said, though what that does for memory over many months is a harder question.

Ravi explained that most of the research on exercise and the brain concerns aerobic activity, which is any steady effort that raises the heart rate and the breathing for a sustained period. Brisk walking, cycling, swimming and dancing all qualify, and nobody has found one clear winner among them. For Leila this was good news, since it meant that the best choice was whichever one she would keep doing.

The brain is threaded with an enormous network of tiny blood vessels, Ravi said, and when they are damaged the brain can suffer. Doctors have found that many of the things which protect the heart, such as regular activity, a healthy blood pressure and not smoking, also seem to protect those delicate vessels. It is a good reminder, he added, that the brain is part of the body and not a separate machine.

Over lunch, Ravi mentioned a protein called BDNF, which scientists believe helps nerve cells to survive, grow and form new connections. In animal experiments, exercise clearly raises its level, and some human studies have found small increases too, but nobody can say yet how much this matters for everyday memory. He made a point of saying that headlines about miracle proteins often run far ahead of the evidence.

Deep inside each side of the brain, Ravi said, lies a curved structure called the hippocampus, which is vital for forming new memories and which tends to shrink a little as we age. A few well-known studies of older adults found that people who walked regularly kept more of it, or even gained a little, than people who stayed inactive. The results are encouraging, he said, but they come from small groups, and larger studies are still needed.

Mice that are given a running wheel, Ravi explained, grow more new brain cells in the hippocampus than mice that are not. Whether adult human beings make many new neurons is still a lively scientific argument, and the answer may depend on the methods used to look for them. He warned Leila not to treat a result in mice as proof about herself.

Many studies find that people who exercise do better on memory tests, but Ravi insisted on the difference between a link and a cause. People who exercise may also eat better, sleep better, earn more or simply feel well enough to be active in the first place, which muddies the picture. To untangle it, he said, scientists use trials in which people are chosen by chance to exercise or not.

In the best trials, people are assigned at random to exercise or to a comparison group and then tested on their thinking over months. The results, Ravi admitted, are more modest and more mixed than the headlines suggest, with some reviews finding small benefits to attention and memory in some adults and others finding very little. Leila liked this honesty, which made her trust the rest of what he said.

When the trials do find a benefit, Ravi told her, it is often in what scientists call executive function, which covers planning, switching between tasks, ignoring distractions and holding several things in mind. These are exactly the skills that a bookkeeper uses to organise a busy day, though the improvements, where found, tend to be small. Leila wrote the phrase on a small card, pleased to have a name for the skills she used every day, and stuck it carefully on her monitor.

By the end of their third walk, Leila realised that her shoulders had dropped and that she had not thought about her keys for an hour. Mood, Ravi told her, is one of the most reliable things exercise seems to change, with many studies showing that people feel calmer and more cheerful afterwards. She noticed that it was also one of the easiest effects to observe for herself.

The popular explanation for the good mood after exercise is that the body releases endorphins, the natural painkillers that make us feel pleasure. Ravi said that this is probably only part of the story, since researchers have also found signs that other chemicals, including some related to cannabis in the body, may contribute. The full picture is still being worked out, which he found exciting rather than disappointing.

When we feel under pressure, Ravi said, the body releases hormones such as cortisol, which prepare us to fight or flee, and which do harm when they stay high for too long. Exercise raises cortisol briefly, as a hard day of work does, but regular activity seems to help the body to settle afterwards and cope better with later stress. Leila, who spent her days chasing deadlines, found this idea so interesting that she asked him to explain it all over again on the way home.

Reviews of many trials have found that regular exercise can reduce symptoms of mild to moderate depression for some people, Ravi told her, and the effect appears to be roughly comparable to some other approaches. He stressed, however, that exercise is not a replacement for professional care, and that anyone who has felt low for weeks should speak to a doctor. This is general information about groups of people, he said, and not advice for any individual, so it cannot tell anyone what their own treatment should be.

On Thursday they took the long way through the town park, where tall trees muffled the noise of the traffic and the air smelled of cut grass. Some studies suggest that walking among greenery lifts mood and eases tension more than walking beside a busy road, although it is hard to separate the effect of the place from the effect of the walk itself. Whatever the explanation turned out to be, Leila decided that she liked it very much and that she would be coming back.

Ravi told her about a growing body of research on the effects of a single session of exercise, which suggests that attention and decision-making can improve for a short while afterwards. Studies in schools have found that children often concentrate better after an active break, although the effects are small and depend on how the breaks are organised. For Leila, who spent hours on columns of figures, the idea of a brisk walk before a difficult task seemed worth testing.

Leila admitted that she sat at her desk for most of eight hours without moving anything but her fingers. Long periods of sitting are linked to poorer health, Ravi said, and researchers are also looking at whether breaking them up improves energy and concentration. His advice was gentle and practical, which was to stand up, stretch and walk for a couple of minutes every half hour.

The next morning Leila set a timer on her phone to ring every thirty minutes, and she felt a little silly doing it. Each time it sounded, she stood up, filled a glass with water, walked once around the office or looked out of the window at the sky. Her colleagues first stared, then asked to join her, and by lunchtime half of them were doing it too.

That week, Leila found that she fell asleep quickly and woke feeling less foggy, and she told Ravi that she suspected the walking. Many studies do suggest that regular activity helps people sleep better, he said, and sleep matters to the brain because it is while we rest that many memories are stored and sorted. In this way, exercise and sleep may well work as a team, each one making the other more effective and both of them looking after the mind.

Ravi found the international guidelines on his phone and read them to her slowly. Adults, the World Health Organization advises, should aim for roughly one hundred and fifty to three hundred minutes of moderate activity each week, together with muscle-strengthening exercises on two or more days. That works out, he calculated, as about half an hour on most days, which sounded to Leila considerably less frightening than she had feared.

How can anyone tell what counts as moderate effort, Leila wondered, without access to a laboratory and a great deal of expensive equipment? Ravi offered an easy rule of thumb, which is that during moderate activity you can talk comfortably but would find singing hard, while vigorous activity leaves you able to say only a few words at a time. They tested the rule that afternoon by humming a song all the way along the canal, and by gasping through the chorus whenever the path went uphill.

Walking was only half of the plan, Ravi said, because muscles also need regular use, and strength is important for staying independent as we age. A number of trials have found that strength training may improve some aspects of thinking in older adults, and the evidence is promising but not yet as strong as for walking. He handed her two bottles of water and showed her how to do slow shoulder presses.

On Tuesday evening Leila climbed the steps of the community hall and joined a class of beginners learning a simple dance. Within five minutes she was remembering a sequence of steps, listening for the beat and trying not to tread on her partner's toes, all at the same time. Ravi, who watched from the doorway, said that this combination of movement, memory and attention is exactly what researchers love to study.

Each time Leila's feet found the right step, Ravi said, her brain was strengthening a pattern of connections that had not existed before. Activities which combine physical effort with learning, such as dancing, tai chi or a new sport, are of particular interest to scientists, although it is not yet clear whether they are better than plain walking. They are, he added with a grin, usually a great deal more fun than counting laps, and enjoyment is a powerful reason to keep going.

Mrs Okoro, who found brisk walking hard on her knees, asked whether gentle exercise could still be worth the effort. Ravi said that slow activities such as tai chi and yoga have been studied, and although the studies are often small, they suggest some benefits for balance, mood and wellbeing. Anything that gets you moving regularly and safely, he added, is a perfectly good place to begin.

Mrs Okoro, who lived next door, was delighted to be invited, and she walked briskly beside them, talking about her grandchildren and her tomato plants. Ravi pointed out that social contact is itself linked to better health in later life, and that exercise taken with friends is easier to keep up. Loneliness, he said, may be a quiet risk for the brain, and a good conversation is a cheap kind of medicine.

Leila had signed up to learn Italian for a holiday in the spring, and she asked Ravi whether exercise could help the words to stick. A few small studies suggest that moderate exercise after studying may help memories to last, he said, but the evidence is early and nobody should treat it as a trick. The sensible conclusion, he suggested, was to study properly, to move regularly, to sleep well and then to repeat the whole cycle.

Ravi suggested an experiment with an audience of one, in which Leila wrote a few lines each evening about her exercise, her sleep and her mood. A diary cannot prove that exercise is the cause of anything, he cautioned, because many things change from week to week, but it does reveal patterns that memory alone tends to hide. Leila bought a green notebook the very next morning, and she began her first entry that evening with the date and a smiling face.

Leila finally asked the question that she had been avoiding, which was whether her forgetfulness was a sign of something serious. Ravi replied that occasional lapses such as lost keys, missing names or a forgotten errand are very common at every age, especially in people who are tired, stressed or busy. If memory problems become worse over time or begin to interfere with daily life, he added, it is sensible to talk to a doctor.

Dementia is a word for a group of conditions that affect memory and thinking, Ravi explained, and it is one of the great worries of later life. Many large studies have found that people who are physically active have a lower risk of developing it, but since these are observations and not proofs, no one can promise that exercise will prevent it. Genes, general health, education and plain chance all play their part as well, which is why he refused to give her any promises.

Exercise is one piece of a larger puzzle, said Ravi, and he counted the other pieces off on his fingers. Doctors who study brain health also point to blood pressure, hearing, not smoking, a lifetime of learning and strong friendships, and they say that the more of these a person looks after, the better. Leila began to see her walks as a part of a bigger picture and not as a single magic cure.

Over supper Ravi warned her against any shop that sells a single food or pill as a brain booster, because the research has so far supported no such miracle. A varied diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains and fish seems to be good for the heart and the brain alike, he said, and a glass of water is no bad idea either. Even mild dehydration, some studies suggest, can make it harder to concentrate, so she promised to keep a bottle on her desk.

On the twentieth day the rain was so heavy that the canal path turned into a stream, and Leila decided that for once she would stay at home. She turned up the radio, danced around her kitchen with a wooden spoon, and then climbed her staircase twenty times, laughing at the sight of herself in the hall mirror. Ravi cheerfully declared the day a total success and promised that the spoon would be mentioned in his next lecture.

At work, there were days when Leila found only ten minutes to spare, and she worried that this was pointless. Ravi reassured her that every bout of movement counts, that short walks add up over a week, and that health organisations stress that some activity is always better than none. The important thing, he said, was to stop thinking of exercise as an all-or-nothing project.

Some studies found that short bursts of very hard exercise raise levels of BDNF and similar substances more than gentle activity does, Ravi told her. The results are far from settled, however, and for most people it is the habit that matters, so the best exercise is the one that you will actually do, week after week. Anyone who wants to try intense exercise, he added, should build up slowly, and should check with a doctor first if they have any health condition.

Before they went any further, Ravi wanted to repeat some safety advice, since he was a student and not a doctor. Anyone who has a health condition, takes regular medicine or has been inactive for many years should ask a doctor before increasing exercise, and everyone should start gently. If you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness, he said, stop at once and get medical help.

Balance is a skill that fades quietly unless we use it, Ravi told Leila, and falls are a serious cause of injury in later life. He taught her a simple exercise, which was to stand on one leg while brushing her teeth, using the sink for support at first and then without. She wobbled for a week, then discovered that she could hold the pose for the full two minutes.

Leila confessed that she had never liked the gym and that the thought of treadmills made her tired. Ravi replied that people stay with exercise for years only when they find something they enjoy, and that enjoyment is a far better motivator than guilt or willpower. So she scrapped the exercises she hated, kept the dancing and the canal, and added a Saturday swim with Mrs Okoro.

Willpower, Ravi said, is a poor foundation for a habit, and a better method is to attach the new behaviour to something that you already do without thinking. Leila decided that her morning coffee would from now on be followed by a walk, and she left her shoes beside the kettle as a reminder. In one study, a new habit took about two months on average to become automatic, though people varied widely.

In the fifth week a heavy cold knocked Leila flat, and for seven days she did nothing more strenuous than lift a teacup. She felt a heavy wave of guilt, as though she had thrown away everything she had built, but Ravi told her that a break from exercise is a normal part of life. When she felt better, she restarted slowly, with a gentle half-hour walk and not a heroic jog.

Looking back through her green notebook, Leila saw that she had not lost her keys for ten days, and that a shopping list and a colleague's name had both come back to her unaided. Ravi was delighted for her, although he gently reminded her that sleep, mood, attention and the novelty of a new routine could each be part of the explanation. Whatever the cause, she felt happier and more like herself than she had in years, and as far as she was concerned that mattered too.

Before he left, Ravi wanted to be quite clear that exercise is not a magic pill and cannot turn an average memory into a brilliant one. Its effects on thinking, as far as we can tell, are modest rather than miraculous, and they work best alongside enough sleep, interesting challenges, good food and good company. A walk, he said, is a very good ingredient, but it is not a complete recipe.

Ravi was cautious about the many apps that promise to train the brain, because the evidence that they improve everyday thinking is weaker than their advertising suggests. Learning a real skill, such as a language, a musical instrument or a craft, keeps the mind engaged, he said, and is likely to bring other rewards besides. Leila's Italian lessons, he joked, were a better investment than any puzzle on a screen.

When the month was over, Ravi shouldered his rucksack and Leila walked him to the station, feeling a lump in her throat. She promised that she would keep up the walks, the dancing and the diary, and he promised to phone every Sunday to hear the results. As the train pulled away, she realised that she was already looking forward to Monday morning.

Back at home, Leila wrote out a weekly plan in green ink and stuck it to the refrigerator, where she could not avoid reading it. It included brisk walks on most days, strength exercises twice a week, her Tuesday dance class, a sensible bedtime and a regular coffee with Mrs Okoro. It was not a dramatic plan, but she knew by now that dramatic plans rarely survive the first rainy day.

On Sunday evening Ravi telephoned, and Leila told him that she had just finished a long walk beside the canal, with the sun going down in red and gold. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot replace a conversation with a doctor who knows your own health and history. Whatever your age, he said, a little movement most days is a kind thing to do for your body and your mind, so go on, put on your shoes.
